subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Dear Amandeep, I am still shaking from this morning. Near the station a man collapsed on the pavement, and about thirty of us were walking past. I slowed down and looked at everyone else. Nobody stopped, so I thought maybe it is not serious, maybe he is drunk, maybe someone has already called. Then I saw his hand twitch and felt sick. I called out, "You, in the blue jacket, call an ambulance!" and the man in the blue jacket froze, then dialled. A woman knelt beside the collapsed man. An ambulance came within minutes. I do not know what happened to him afterwards. But I know how close I came to walking on. — Noor

qa.q: About how many people were walking past the man who collapsed?
qa.a: About thirty people were walking past.

qa.q: Why did Noor think it might not be serious when nobody stopped?
qa.a: Noor read the crowd's inaction as a sign it was not serious, each person taking the others' calm as proof; the twitching hand broke that belief and brought a sick feeling.

qa.q: What turning point led Noor to act?
qa.a: Noor saw the man's hand twitch, felt sick, and called out to one person in a blue jacket to phone an ambulance instead of waiting.

qa.q: What might the man in the blue jacket have been feeling when Noor called out?
qa.a: The man in the blue jacket probably felt startled and suddenly responsible; being named pulled him out of the crowd's passive waiting, and he dialled.

grounding: A commuter sees someone collapse while the crowd keeps walking, each reading the others' inaction as proof it is not serious.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Simran, listen, it's Jasleen, and I need to say what I saw. Last night on the market road a man kept following a woman and shouting things at her, and there were maybe twenty people around: the tea stall, two rickshaw drivers, some couples. Everyone kept walking, and so did I. All those calm faces made me think it was not serious. She was gripping her bag and walking faster. I turned around after twenty steps, walked up to the tea vendor and said loudly, "Please call the police helpline." Then the two rickshaw drivers stood near her. The man slunk off. I am shaking even now.

qa.q: How many people were around when the man followed the woman?
qa.a: There were maybe twenty people around.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen keep walking even though the woman was gripping her bag?
qa.a: Jasleen took the calm faces of the crowd as proof it was not serious, an assumption shared by everyone; afterwards the shaking shows how uneasy that decision felt.

qa.q: What choice made Jasleen turn around after twenty steps, and what did that action achieve?
qa.a: Jasleen turned back, spoke loudly to the tea vendor to call the police helpline, and this drew the rickshaw drivers to stand near the woman until the man left.

qa.q: What might the woman have been feeling while everyone walked past?
qa.a: The woman was probably frightened and alone, gripping her bag and walking faster while the crowd's silence gave her no sign anyone would help.

grounding: A commuter sees a woman harassed while the crowd keeps walking, and pluralistic ignorance makes each person read others' inaction as proof it is not serious.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
I'm Disha. I was coming up the metro stairs at Rajiv Chowk that evening when I saw him: an older man in a grey sweater, sitting down suddenly against the wall, then sliding sideways.
People kept walking. Dozens. A man stepped over his bag. I slowed down, and I remember thinking, if it were serious, surely someone would stop. Everyone looked so calm.
Then a woman in office clothes, Alka, her ID card said, knelt beside him. “Uncle? Uncle, can you hear me?” She looked up and caught my eye. “Can you get the station staff?”
I ran. The staff came with a wheelchair and called an ambulance.
Afterwards I stood there shaking, thinking how close I came to walking past because nobody else stopped.

qa.q: Where did the man sit down suddenly?
qa.a: Against the wall on the metro stairs at Rajiv Chowk.

qa.q: What was Disha thinking before Alka knelt?
qa.a: Disha felt unsure and read the crowd's calm as a sign it wasn't serious, since surely someone would stop if it were.

qa.q: What worked once Alka stepped in?
qa.a: Alka checked on the man and asked Disha directly to get station staff, which turned a watcher into a helper.

qa.q: How might the man have been affected by the crowd walking past?
qa.a: He was left alone at a dangerous moment, since each person took the others' walking as proof he was fine.

grounding: A commuter recalls seeing a man collapse while the crowd walked on, reading their inaction as proof it wasn't serious, until one person acted.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
Monday: At Dadar station, Vijay saw a man following a young woman, Dolma, too closely, muttering at her. She walked faster. Hundreds of people pushed past. Nobody looked twice. Vijay thought, if it were bad, someone would do something. He caught his train.
Wednesday: He saw her again on the same platform, alone, glancing over her shoulder. The same man was near the stairs. Vijay's chest tightened. He walked over and stood beside her. “Everything okay? Want me to walk you to the ladies' coach?”
Dolma let out a long breath. “Yes. Please.” The man turned away. Vijay pointed him out to the railway police constable at the gate, who went after him.
Friday: Vijay kept thinking about Monday, and how the crowd's calm had fooled him.

qa.q: Which station were they at?
qa.a: They were at Dadar station.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling on Wednesday when he saw the man again?
qa.a: His chest tightened; he felt anxious and alarmed, and this time he trusted his own concern over the crowd.

qa.q: What did Vijay do on Wednesday that helped?
qa.a: He stood beside Dolma, offered to walk her to the ladies' coach, and pointed the man out to the railway police.

qa.q: How might Dolma have felt on Monday as the crowd pushed past?
qa.a: She probably felt frightened and alone, being followed while hundreds of people acted as if nothing was happening.

grounding: Shows a commuter who first reads the crowd's inaction as proof a woman's harassment isn't serious, then later steps in.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
Noor, you asked why I always stop when someone falls on the road. Let me tell you. I'm your Nilesh chacha, and this is from Delhi, when I was twenty-five.
It was a hot afternoon at the ITO bus stop. A man in a safari suit went down, just folded onto the footpath. Maybe forty of us were there.
And you know what I did? I looked at everyone else. Nobody moved, so I thought, must be nothing, maybe he's drunk. Everybody was thinking the same thing, looking at each other.
Then a college girl screamed, “Why is nobody helping?” It broke the spell. Five of us rushed at once. Someone called an ambulance.
He lived. But I never forgot how forty calm faces almost fooled me.

qa.q: How many people were at the bus stop?
qa.a: Maybe forty people were there.

qa.q: How did young Nilesh feel when he looked at everyone else?
qa.a: He felt unsure, and the calm faces made him think it must be nothing, so he held back.

qa.q: What turning point in the story got people moving?
qa.a: A college girl screaming "Why is nobody helping?" broke the spell, and five people rushed to help.

qa.q: How might the college girl have felt before she screamed?
qa.a: She was probably alarmed and frustrated, seeing a man collapse while forty adults just stood there.

grounding: An elder recalls a man collapsing at a bus stop and a crowd, himself included, reading each other's inaction as proof it wasn't serious.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
Monsoon rain hammered the railway footbridge at 6:15, and the 6:22 fast was Naveen's last chance to reach home before his daughter's school play.
Halfway across, a woman in a green saree sat down suddenly against the railing, then slid sideways, her bag spilling. People stepped around her, umbrellas tilted. Nobody stopped.
Naveen slowed. Maybe she's just tired, he thought. If it were serious, someone would be helping. A man glanced down at her, then glanced at the crowd, and kept walking. That glance caught Naveen: everyone was reading everyone else.
He turned back and knelt. "Madam? Can you hear me?" Her eyes fluttered. "Lakshmi," she whispered. "Dizzy."
Naveen called for an ambulance, then waved to a railway police constable at the stairs. The 6:22 thundered below. He stayed, holding his umbrella over her, until the stretcher came.

qa.q: Which train was Naveen trying to catch?
qa.a: The 6:22 fast.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when he first slowed down?
qa.a: Naveen felt unsure and hesitant, taking the calm crowd as proof it wasn't serious, and anxious about missing his train.

qa.q: What helped Naveen break out of the crowd's pattern?
qa.a: Noticing the man glance at the crowd instead of the woman showed him everyone was copying each other, so he checked for himself.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Lakshmi as people stepped around her?
qa.a: Lakshmi was probably frightened and helpless, dizzy on a wet bridge while umbrellas passed by.

grounding: Shows a commuter who sees a woman collapse while the crowd walks on, each person reading the others' calm as proof it is not serious.
